title: Face-to-face psychotherapy as a straw man in trials of therapist-guided internet interventions: A re-analysis of treatment integrity
abstract: Abstract Three meta-analyses have synthesized trials that directly compared 2 modalities of cognitive-behavior therapy: Therapist-guided internet intervention (iCBT) versus face-to-face psychotherapy (fCBT). These meta-analyses have concluded that iCBT has similar effects as fCBT across various disorders. However, it remains unclear whether the included trials have implemented fCBT according to minimum criteria of treatment integrity. This research presents a re-analysis of treatment integrity of trials included in the most recent meta-analysis (Hedmann-Lagerlöf et al., 2023). We included 23 trials out of the original 31 trials. We coded 3 key criteria of treatment integrity: (1) Use of full-length evidence-based treatment manual; (2) use of professional therapists; (3) specific training for therapists. Only 2 trials (8.7%) out of the included 23 trials fulfilled all three treatment integrity criteria. Eleven trials (47.8%) fulfilled 0 or 1 criterion. The results of the 2 trials that fulfilled minimum treatment integrity criteria showed an advantage for fCBT, in the magnitude of a small to moderate effect size (SMD=0.37, 95% CI [0.13, 0.62], p=0.003, I 2=0%). Our re-analysis suggests that fCBT in iCBT trials is typically implemented in a restricted way that does neither meet methodological standards nor evidence-based recommendations for good clinical practice. Thus, currently available trials provide no evidence for the claim that iCBT and fCBT have comparable effects. If anything, the scarce available evidence suggests a superiority of face-to-face psychotherapy.
